articles.title: California buried about 270,000 waste tyres beneath a highway near Confusion Hill; the rubber became lightweight fill for two new bridges
articles.summary: A California highway project found an unusual use for thousands of discarded tyres.
articles.body: A California highway project found an unusual use for thousands of discarded tyres. In 2009, the California Department of Transportation completed a road repair project at Confusion Hill on US 101 in Mendocino County, where longstanding rockslides had repeatedly threatened the highway. The new route bypassed the unstable area using two bridges, but engineers faced another problem, adding conventional fill would have placed too much weight on an underground drainage structure beneath one bridge embankment. Instead, they turned to tyre-derived aggregate (TDA), made from shredded waste tyres, as a lightweight fill material. The project ultimately used about 270,000 waste tyres, giving the discarded rubber a structural role beneath the road.Confusion Hill's rockslides had threatened US 101 for yearsThe Confusion Hill project addressed a longstanding problem along US 101 near Piercy in Mendocino County. According to CalRecycle, rockslides had occurred in the area for thousands of years and had affected the highway for at least 17 years before the project. Roadway slip-outs had become more frequent, while falling debris and slope movement caused repeated closures and maintenance problems. In 2001 alone, roadway stabilisation work cost $3.2 million. Engineers needed a more reliable route through the slide area that would keep US 101 open to traffic. The solution was to bypass the unstable section with two new bridges rather than continue relying on repeated repairs to the existing route.Engineers needed a fill material that would not overload the groundThe bridge route created a separate engineering challenge. CalRecycle says the north bridge embankment sat above an existing underground drainage structure that could not handle the additional load created by raising the embankment. Engineers therefore needed a material that could provide the necessary fill while adding less weight than conventional soil or rock. Tire-derived aggregate was selected for the job because it is lightweight and cost-effective. TDA is produced by processing waste tyres into pieces of rubber and is used in civil engineering applications including road repairs, embankments and slope stabilisation. TDA can weigh about one-third as much as soil and other similar construction materials, making it useful where excessive loading could cause problems.About 270,000 waste tyres went beneath the highwayFor the Confusion Hill project, the existing fill material over the underground structures was removed and replaced with lightweight tire-derived aggregate. CalRecycle also records that the project used approximately 270,000 waste tyres and was completed in 2009. The tyres were not simply buried whole; they were processed into TDA and used as engineered fill within the road project. The work was a lightweight-fill project for rockslide and road repair, with the TDA incorporated into the embankment stabilisation. This turned a large quantity of waste tyres into a construction material while addressing the weight limitations around the drainage structure beneath the bridge embankment.The project showed how old tyres can become infrastructure materialConfusion Hill became one example of California's wider use of tire-derived aggregate in civil engineering. TDA is a material that can be used for lightweight fill behind retaining walls, road repairs and embankment construction, as well as for drainage and vibration mitigation. Its lightweight and free-draining properties can make it useful where conventional fill would create excessive loads or other engineering difficulties. The state's project profiles include other applications involving hundreds of thousands of waste tyres. Rather than sending every discarded tyre to disposal, projects such as Confusion Hill demonstrate how processed rubber can become part of infrastructure. articles.title: Two Renoir paintings recovered after France museum heist, mayor says
articles.summary: The recovered Renoir paintings, valued at millions, were stolen in a daring heist at Cagnes-sur-Mer last month.
articles.body:
Two paintings by the French Impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir that were stolen from a museum in southern France a month ago have been recovered, the town’s mayor said.

“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city’s history,” Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, said on Friday. “Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief.”

Six people have been arrested in connection with the theft, local authorities said. Masson did not say where the paintings were found or in what condition.

Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum a little before 6am on September 8, cutting through a fence to enter the grounds, smashing a window and using an electric saw to cut the clips securing the frames, Masson said at the time.

He described them as “well equipped” and “well informed”.

The museum alarm sounded at 5:48am, and municipal police arrived five minutes later, forcing the thieves to flee.

They had taken four paintings, valued by the mayor at about nine million euros ($10.5m).

Two of the stolen works – Renoir’s “Portrait of Madame Pichon” and “Coco Reading” – were later found dropped in the museum garden, the prosecutor’s office said at the time.

The two works that remained missing were “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano” and “Young Woman at the Well”, the office said.

Police said last month that the thieves were not first-time offenders and had scoped out the premises.

The Marseille prosecutor opened a theft investigation into an organised gang, and the national office for trafficking in cultural goods joined the probe.

The museum, opened in 1960, is in the painter’s last home, where he died in 1919.

“This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums,” Masson said after the robbery.

The theft came less than a year after jewels worth about $100m were stolen from the Louvre in Paris in a daylight robbery.

The four suspected robbers have been arrested, but the jewels have not been found.

In August, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m that were stolen from a museum in March.

articles.title: Putin tells Trump peace talks are unlikely, cites Ukraine drone attacks
articles.summary: Drone attacks on Moscow during last month’s election undermined trilateral peace negotiations, the Kremlin says.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said an immediate resumption of peace talks with Ukraine is unlikely, citing drone attacks on Moscow during parliamentary elections last month.

In a phone call with US President Donald Trump on Friday, Putin said Moscow was ready to resume negotiations with Kyiv after the parliamentary elections. However, the drone attacks on the capital made the resumption of trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US unlikely.

“By launching a large-scale drone attack on Moscow, other cities and polling stations on the most important day of the elections, and by targeting some people involved in organising the elections, the Kyiv regime has, in reality, interrupted the possibility of an immediate resumption of the negotiation process,” said Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov about the call with Trump.

“As the president said, we will now assess when these negotiations can resume,” he added regarding the trilateral talks.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday that Russia’s war in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate and the United States will keep working towards a deal to end the war.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier this week that the country was ready to hold trilateral talks with the United States and Russia this month.

Earlier on Friday, Donald Trump announced after the call with Putin that Russia agreed to deliver more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to American and global markets.

The deal was criticised by US lawmakers, Zelenskyy and European allies.

Zelenskyy called the agreement a “gift to Putin”.

“All that money goes toward the war against people, against Ukraine, against all of us. I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair,” he said in a statement.

In response to the US-Russia diesel deal, a government spokesperson said the United Kingdom would continue to “maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK.”

articles.title: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
articles.summary: The storm took direct aim at Florida and is expected to impact Alabama, Georgia, and Louisiana.
articles.body:
Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate.

The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening.

Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas.

Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean.

Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm.

In Florida, those evacuations include coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"

Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.

Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.

It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October.

The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned.

After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday.

As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).

The Florida Panhandle and the rest of the US Gulf Coast are facing fierce winds and heavy rain as the hurricane barrels down. There is also the potential for accompanying tornadoes, Melissa Watson, a Florida-based meteorologist at the National Weather Service told the BBC.

For those who have not evacuated, "the main thing will be having multiple ways to receive warnings" about tornadoes and storm surges, Watson said. "If you are near the coast, being able to move to higher ground," is also essential in the event of storm surges.

"We want people to be safe, so don't go out there trying to look for damage ... to post on social media," she added. "We want people to remain inside and safe while the hurricane is moving through."

Even before the storm made landfall, hundreds of thousands were without power in the country's southeast - and Alabama, Florida and Georgia have issued states of emergency as they brace for heavy rains and flooding.

More than 350,000 were in the dark in Florida and another 170,000 in Alabama saw outages, according to PowerOutage.us.

The hurricane's winds are expected to be felt further inland in Georgia, albeit at a lesser intensity, where already about 8,000 customers were without power.

People on the coast of the Florida panhandle have been told to seek immediate shelter under an "Extreme Wind Warning".

Some Florida officials have ordered residents to "Get out NOW!", urging people to follow evacuation orders.

John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left.

"It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said.

"Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said

Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over".

A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes".

Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home.

People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this".

One indicator of a storm's severity to communities in the southern US is whether the stalwart restaurant chain The Waffle House would close its doors to customers. On Friday, it did.

A Waffle House spokesperson confirmed to the BBC that the chain had already closed a number of locations in the hurricane's path and "will continue monitoring conditions".

US President Donald Trump said he will no longer attend a major American football college game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama because of the hurricane, shifting plans to attend a rally in Tennessee instead.

Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend.

Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters.

Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific.

While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California.

Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide.

Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides".

It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding.

With additional reporting by Simon King.

articles.title: US country music star Ella Langley cancels Tulsa show over 'security threat'
articles.summary: Police say they checked the concert venue in Tulsa, Oklahoma but "could not find any threat".
articles.body:
US country music star Ella Langley has said she had to cancel her sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night, due to a "serious security threat".

The singer made what she called the "incredibly difficult" decision around two hours before the show at the 19,000-seater arena was due to start.

In a post on Instagram, the 27-year-old said the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff and my team".

Cpt Richard Meulenberg from Tulsa Police Department said a person had called saying "great harm" would be done at the event with "shots fired and bombs."

He stated his team had checked the venue at BOK Center several times before the show and "could not find any threat".

"The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made.

"We could not find a credible threat," he said, stressing that the person who had made the call "disrupted this entire event" for thousands of Langley fans.

The star - who did not give any further details - also apologised to her fans, saying additional information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible".

BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed.

"We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend."

In September, Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas overtook Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history.

Its success helped the singer from Alabama to sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May.

articles.title: ‘Zimmedari uthao badalne ki’: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke to reach Delhi around 10am for ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke left the Four Seasons Hotel in Mumbai on Saturday morning for the airport to travel to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke left the Four Seasons Hotel in Mumbai on Saturday morning for the airport to travel to Delhi, where the party has called for a protest at Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Dipke is expected to reach Delhi by 10am, a CJP functionary said, according to news agency PTI.In a post on X, Dipke wrote, "Zindagi jeene ke do hi tarike hote hain, ek jo ho raha hai hone do, bardaasht karte jao, ya phir zimmedari uthao use badalne ki."A few protesters were detained near Janpath in the Connaught Place area on Saturday as the CJP called for a ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ demonstration demanding Kumar’s removal.The Delhi Police has denied permission for the protest, citing the possibility of "serious" law-and-order concerns and inconvenience to residents and citizens.Delhi Police denies permission for CJP protestIn a letter addressed to CJP co-convenor Saurav Das and joint secretary Balkrishna, the deputy commissioner of police, New Delhi district, said granting permission could lead to serious law-and-order issues."In the larger public interest, the permission sought cannot be granted and is hereby denied," the letter stated.The police said the communication received from the party was merely an intimation and not a duly submitted application seeking permission. According to the letter, applications to hold programmes at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days before the proposed date.The police also cited previous instances of alleged violations of protest conditions, including demonstrations continuing beyond stipulated time limits, which had resulted in law-and-order issues.Despite the denial, CJP has called for a large mobilisation at Jantar Mantar. “10th October. Jantar Mantar 2.0. We’re coming together again to raise our voice against Gyanesh Kumar. Thousands of us are expected...,” the party said in an Instagram post.35,000 security personnel deployed across DelhiDelhi has tightened security across the capital to prevent protesters from gathering at Jantar Mantar. Checks have been intensified at the city's borders, roads barricaded and mobile internet services suspended in parts of central Delhi.More than 35,000 Delhi Police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the national capital amid heightened security arrangements. Officials estimate that around 20,000 people could attempt to reach the protest site.Police sources said additional forces had been sought because the turnout during the CJP's protest in June-July had been “underestimated”.Mobile internet services within a 4km radius of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing were suspended at 10pm on Friday. The restrictions are scheduled to remain in force until 10pm on Saturday.The entry and exit gates of 57 metro stations were initially ordered to be closed, with the number later reduced to 45. The restrictions followed a communication from the Delhi Police's Transport Range to the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation, citing the possibility of “unruly crowd movement towards sensitive locations”.The police have instructed their teams to detain anyone attempting to stage a protest, irrespective of their location. Central Armed Police Forces units have also been directed not to issue weapons for deployment related to the demonstration, with letters sent to the concerned directorates regarding the allotment plan.Unlike the deployment during the INDIA bloc protest, police teams have been authorised to carry lathis and batons. In view of alleged deliberate attempts to record and circulate videos portraying police personnel in a negative light, teams have been instructed to avoid verbal confrontations with protesters.Those detained are to be taken to six designated centres: Chhatrasal Stadium, Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, Yamuna Sports Complex, Surajmal Stadium, the community centre in Daulatpur and the community centre in Pandrawal.Additional women personnel from Uttar Pradesh and Haryana have also been called in. Multiple facial recognition systems, additional CCTV cameras, rooftop spotters and drones are expected to be deployed across central Delhi.Several student outfits and political groups are also expected to join the demonstration.Dipke says he will not back down if arrestedOn Friday, Dipke said he would not withdraw from the protest even if he were detained or arrested. In a video posted on X, he urged people to participate in large numbers while maintaining peace and discipline.He said he planned to leave Mumbai on Saturday morning and was uncertain whether he would be arrested at the airport or later.Dipke said the party's demands included free and fair elections, Kumar's resignation, scrapping the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and an independent selection procedure for Election Commissioners.“So my only request to all of you is that in case I am detained or in case I am arrested, I have no fear of that. If this government wants to invoke the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) against me, the National Security Act (NSA), or whatever they want to invoke, you can do so. But what I am fighting for, what CJP is fighting for, is free and fair elections.""We need free and fair elections, and those elections cannot happen without the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, cannot happen without scrapping SIR, and cannot happen without an independent selection procedure through which Election Commissioners are selected. That process needs to be neutral and independent. Without that, free and fair elections cannot happen,” he said.Calling the demonstration a fight to protect democracy, Dipke appealed to participants to ensure that it remained peaceful and non-violent. He urged them to follow the law and avoid actions that could undermine the protest.“This is a fight to save the country's democracy. Therefore, all of you, please come to Delhi's Jantar Mantar tomorrow in large numbers. But again, my request to everyone is—remember, we are law-abiding citizens, we are peaceful citizens. So no mistake should be made from our end. We are not goons,” Dipke said.Centre asks states and UTs to coordinate with Delhi PoliceThe proposed mobilisation has also prompted the Union home ministry to direct states and Union Territories to strengthen security arrangements.In an official letter, Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan asked police chiefs of all states and Union Territories to coordinate with Delhi Police and take preventive measures in view of the proposed gathering. The communication cited concerns over a possible attempt by CJP and its supporters to enter the national capital despite the denial of permission.“I write to draw your immediate attention to the grave law & order and public order implications arising from a proposed mass mobilisation by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, scheduled for 10.10.2026. Vide an official order issued by the Delhi Police, dated 09.10.2026 (copy enclosed), the request submitted on behalf of the CJP has been categorically rejected, and the proposed assembly stands prohibited,” the letter read.The security preparations come amid wider Opposition protests against the SIR exercise and allegations of electoral irregularities.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.summary: The co-pilot and alleged hijacker of a flydubai flight and crash it into Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport was inspired by the September 11, 2001, terror
articles.body: The co-pilot and alleged hijacker of a flydubai flight and crash it into Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport was inspired by the September 11, 2001, terror attacks in the US, according to preliminary findings released by the United Arab Emirates (UAE).Hamam al-Hammami, 29, who was serving as the co-pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on September 30, allegedly planned to take control of the aircraft and crash it into the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport, Israel’s main international airport.According to a statement by UAE attorney general Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, shared by Emirati state media, al-Hammami wanted to carry out an attack similar to the 9/11 attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people in the US 25 years ago. Four commercial planes were hijacked during those attacks and crashed at three locations.“The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his mind, which, according to his confessions, was connected to his decision to pursue a career in aviation,” Friday’s statement said.The co-pilot allegedly planned “a premeditated plot with a terrorist objective, aimed at taking control of the aircraft and using it to carry out a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport,” with the aim of causing “the greatest possible number of casualties,” the statement added.Flew to Israel twice before alleged attackThe preliminary investigation found that the September 30 flight was not al-Hammami’s first trip to Ben Gurion Airport. He had reportedly taken part in two earlier flights to the airport to familiarise himself with the route and the airport before carrying out the alleged attack.An Israeli official and another source familiar with the matter had earlier told CNN that the suspected hijacker likely intended to target the airport, Israel’s main international gateway.The alleged hijacking attempt was stopped after the captain and several passengers restrained al-Hammami and regained control of the aircraft.How the co-pilot became radicalisedThe UAE investigation found that al-Hammami began moving towards extremism and terrorism in 2017, while studying in Australia. He was reportedly influenced by extremist publications and online content that praised terrorist groups and suicide attacks.According to the statement, he “prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out his plot by increasing his exposure to material inciting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach.”Investigators also examined his employment history with different airlines.Al-Hammami worked for Oman Air from 2020 to 2024. He joined Royal Air Maroc in 2025 but worked there for only a few months before moving to Flydubai in January 2026, according to the UAE statement.A source had earlier told CNN that Oman Air removed al-Hammami from flight training because of concerns about his radical views and assigned him another role at the airline.In a statement to the Associated Press last week, Royal Air Maroc said al-Hammami had undergone three months of training with the airline in 2025 as part of its pre-employment process but was not selected for a job.Flydubai recruitment procedures under scrutinyThe UAE investigation also examined how Flydubai hired al-Hammami. Investigators found that he had met the professional and security requirements for the job, including holding a pilot’s licence, possessing a certificate of good conduct and passing the required examinations.“There were “no indications emerging during those procedures that revealed his extremist inclinations or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot,” attorney general Al Shamsi said, according to Emirati state media.Al-Hammami told investigators that he had acted alone, but authorities are still checking his claim.You use AI every day. articles.title: Who is Nidal Hasan? What to know about US plans to livestream an execution online
articles.summary: The planned firing-squad execution on 3 December has led to questions about legality and purpose.
articles.body:
The US Department of Defense plans to livestream on the internet the execution of a convicted killer, a move that has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum.

Former US Army Major Nidal Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on 3 December. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said showing the killing online would act as a deterrent against future attacks.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he approved of the plan but a determination still needed to be made. If it happens as planned, it would be the first-ever broadcast of a US execution.

The decision to show the graphic death has led to condemnations and questions about legality.

Nidal Hasan, a former US Army major and psychiatrist from Virginia, is due to be put to death on 3 December.

John Galligan, a civilian lawyer advising Hasan, said that he was the first person to inform Hasan of the date of his sentence after seeing a social media post about it from the Pentagon's chief spokesman this week.

Galligan told the BBC that the event is being treated like a "carnival" and is the "closest thing to a lynch mob mentality that we used to see in the olden days".

Hasan, a native of Virginia, admitted to fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers in a crowded medical building on Fort Hood, a US military base in Texas, in 2009.

He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.

Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.

The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.

In addition to the 13 troops who died, 32 others were injured in the attack.

It remains unclear whether any restrictions would be implemented on a livestream to limit who can watch the execution. Rules about how executions are carried out and who can watch vary by state, and the military also has its own rules.

A number of states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many require journalists to be present. Some states allow the person being executed to invite people, and some allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses.

Under US Army Regulation 190-55 which governs military executions, only certain categories of people, such as journalists and relatives, are permitted to be present. People aged under 18 are excluded.

Critics of the plan to livestream Hasan's death say it will be hard, if not impossible, to prevent children from watching it live or in recordings afterwards.

One survivor of the Fort Hood attack told the BBC that he opposed livestreaming the execution due to concerns about the message it might send to young people.

Alonzo Lunsford, a former US Army sergeant who was shot seven times, said it should only be viewable by victims and their families.

"As far as the families of the fallen and the families of the survivors, and the survivors themselves, yes, I think we should be able to look at it uncensored," he said.

While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly.

Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.

The UN warned on Friday that livestreaming the execution would "constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment" that is banned under international law.

UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said during Friday's press briefing in New York that the "possibility of…a government executing someone in public or in front of live cameras, frankly, is abhorrent".

It's unclear how or where the US military plans to transmit the stream, and whether it would violate US laws or regulations. Legal challenges are expected in any case.

Truth Social, the social media platform owned by President Trump, does not have a livestream video feature for users.

The White House maintains official accounts and channels on the most widely used online platforms that are capable of streaming live video, namely Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X.

All of the platforms have prohibitions in place on not only violent images and videos, but those that show death or otherwise glorify or make spectacle of violence.

Meta - owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads - explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment.

YouTube, owned by Google, bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers", but says exceptions may be made for "content that is in the public interest".

TikTok has a similar blanket ban. Its policy reads, "We don't allow extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content—especially when it could cause viewers emotional distress." That includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual".

Two weeks ago, TikTok updated its policy to include a possible exception to the prohibition for graphic content that is in the "public interest".

Why is there a planned public execution now?

Several US states allow capital punishment to be carried out by firing squad, or by electrocution.

Most executions are done by lethal injection of multiple drugs. Those drugs are now in short supply, however, due to concerns from drugmakers about how they are being used.

The recent attempted execution of convicted killer Christa Pike in Tennessee failed for reasons that are still under investigation. Some have questioned the age of the drugs that were used.

In the wake of Pike's failed execution, officials are now questioning what other methods may be available to kill condemned prisoners.

The Pentagon announced on 5 October - five days after Pike's botched injections - that Hasan would die by firing squad. Trump approved of the plan, and said he also approved livestreaming the execution, but a final determination had not been made.

Vice-President JD Vance, meanwhile, cast doubt that it would happen, saying he was not sure, and in any case, did not plan to watch.

I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's

When was the last public execution in the US?

The last public execution in the US was the killing of Roscoe "Red" Jackson which took place in front of about 500 people inside a building Missouri, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks US executions.

The most recent widely watched and notable one took place in Kentucky in 1936. Rainey Bethea, convicted of rape, was hanged in front of an outdoor audience estimated at around 20,000 people.

Hasan's execution would be the first by the US military since 1961, and the first execution by firing squad since World War Two.

A US Army private was hanged in 1961 after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl.

A young US Army deserter died by firing squad in January 1945 during the final months of WW2.

articles.title: Three men found guilty in the 2024 killing of Australian and US surfers in Mexico
articles.summary: A local judge on Friday found three Mexicans guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.
articles.body: A local judge on Friday found three Mexicans guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California. The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded Friday after Judge Raúl Hernández in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, alias “El Kekas,” Irineo Francisco “N,” and Ángel Jesús “N” were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson and American Carter Redd Rhoad. The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking. “Today’s guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons, Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad, whose lives were so cruelly taken from them in 2024,” said father Martin Robinson. The three traveled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 80 kilometers (50 miles) from Ensenada, they were reported missing. Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well. García, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Irineo Francisco “N,” and Ángel Jesús “N.” During the month-long trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that García confessed to her that he arrived at the tent where the foreigners were staying with a 9mm pistol. Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them, and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said. The state prosecutor’s office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and “instigated one of her companions to rob them,” which was carried out the following day. The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims’ cell phones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to “aggravated robbery with violence” and “vehicle theft with violence” in an expedited proceeding. However, García and his two accomplices decided to go to trial. The judge will announce the final sentence on Oct. 16. The Baja California State Attorney General’s Office requested for each defendant the “exemplary sentence” of 210 years in prison. “No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honoring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were,” said Martin Robinson. “They will never be forgotten.”

Prosecutor Raul Gerardo Cobo Montejano leaves the Baja California State Palace of Justice, where four individuals appeared in court on charges related to the murder of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend Carter Rhoad, in Ensenada, Mexico, on July 25, 2025.

articles.title: Netflix layoffs: Company may cut  850 jobs; co-CEO Ted Sarandos had said: We’re not growing as fast as…
articles.summary: Netflix is preparing to lay off about 5% of its employees as part of a wider restructuring, according to a report by Puck News.
articles.body: Netflix is preparing to lay off about 5% of its employees as part of a wider restructuring, according to a report by Puck News. Sources told the publication the announcement could come as early as next week, with the streamer under pressure over slowing viewer engagement and a share price that has slid through the year. It would be Netflix’s biggest round of job cuts in four years, and it would land just days before the company reports its third-quarter earnings on October 20.The numbers add up quickly. Puck puts Netflix's global headcount at roughly 17,000, which means around 850 jobs could go. The company's own annual filing listed about 16,000 full-time employees at the end of 2025, so the final number may be closer to 800. It is still unclear which teams will be hit hardest.Netflix's biggest job cuts since 2022 arrive ahead of Q3 earningsIf the cuts go ahead, they will be Netflix's largest since 2022. That year, the streamer lost 200,000 subscribers in a single quarter, its first such drop in more than a decade. It let go of about 150 staff in May and roughly 300 more in June. Smaller rounds have followed, including several dozen roles in its global product team earlier this year.The stock has fallen more than 40% over the past year. Puck links the pressure to last year’s failed bid for Warner Bros and to engagement that grew just 2% in the first half of 2026. The news also lands as layoffs spread across the media business, with Disney cutting jobs three times this year.Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted as much at a Bloomberg event last month. "Overall, we're not growing as fast as I want us to," he said. He also flagged live programming as a drag on the numbers, saying it takes up about 5% of the content budget while drawing roughly 1% of total viewing.Netflix's costs are growing faster than its revenueNetflix is still growing. Revenue rose 13% to $12.6 billion in the April to June quarter. Spending outside content grew faster, though. Marketing, technology and administrative costs together climbed 18% to around $2.3 billion. Technology and development alone jumped 22%, mostly because of a $142 million rise in personnel costs.Headcount kept climbing too, with about 2,000 full-time employees added through 2025. Revenue growth, meanwhile, has cooled from 18% in the last quarter of 2025 to 16% and then 13% this year. Netflix expects around 12% for the September quarter, but it is still targeting a 31.5% operating margin for 2026, up from 29.5% last year.Cutting staff won't touch content, Netflix's biggest expense. It does bring overheads closer in line with slowing sales, and it gives Sarandos and co-CEO Greg Peters a cost story to tell on October 20. Investors will also want to hear how ads, live events and gaming are meant to pick up the growth.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Schoolboy asks Tukaram Mundhe to bring back vada pav in schools; the Maharashtra FDA chief’s response is winning hearts
articles.summary: A school canteen without vada pav may not sound like good news to many children.
articles.body: A school canteen without vada pav may not sound like good news to many children. But when a young student asked Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe to bring back the popular snack, his answer turned into a lesson on food and growing up. A video of their interaction has gone viral on Instagram, drawing attention to the state's efforts to make school food healthier.What the schoolboy asked Tukaram MundheThe boy approached Mundhe with a straightforward request. “Vada pav has been banned in schools, but my friends and I want it back. What do you have to say?”Instead of dismissing the child's demand, the commissioner smiled and explained why children needed to look beyond their favourite snacks.“Our life won’t stop if we don’t eat vada pav. On the contrary, if you eat good nutritious food, you will grow much better,” Mundhe told him.His response was firm without being harsh. The exchange also highlighted a familiar challenge for parents and schools: helping children understand why some everyday food choices deserve a second thought.Why Mundhe warned against fried snacksMundhe advised the student to avoid deep-fried snacks and focus on nutritious food, particularly protein-rich options.Children need a balanced diet that includes protein, carbohydrates, healthy fats, vitamins and minerals. Dal, beans, milk, curd, eggs and other protein-rich foods can contribute to healthy growth.The point is not that one vada pav will harm a child. What matters more is the overall eating pattern and how often less nutritious foods replace balanced meals.ID@undefined Caption not available.ID@undefined Caption not available.His response to the question about Chinese street foodThe conversation did not end with vada pav. The boy also asked about Chinese street food.Mundhe cautioned him about artificial colours and chemicals that may be used in some food preparations. He urged the student to prioritise health over taste.Food safety concerns are worth taking seriously, particularly when ingredients and preparation methods are unclear. However, not all Chinese-style food is unsafe. The hygiene of the vendor, the quality of ingredients and the use of permitted food additives all matter.The exchange offered a simple message: children should learn to enjoy food while also understanding what goes into it.What Maharashtra's school food directive saysMundhe's advice comes amid a statewide drive against high-fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) foods in and around schools.The directive targets products such as vada pav, samosas, burgers, pizzas, chips and aerated drinks in school canteens and within a 50-metre radius of school campuses. It applies across school types and educational boards in Maharashtra.Healthier alternatives include poha, upma, idli, dosa, fresh fruit and buttermilk, alongside balanced meals that meet children's nutritional needs.Disclaimer: This article is for general informational purposes. Nutritional needs vary by age and individual circumstances. articles.title: Kenya prepared for Ebola. It still slipped through — a warning of wider cross-border spread
articles.summary: Kenya had spent months preparing for Ebola, one of the world’s deadliest viral diseases, screening hundreds of thousands of travelers and training nearly 5,000 health workers in case it crossed the borders.
articles.body: Kenya had spent months preparing for Ebola, one of the world’s deadliest viral diseases, screening hundreds of thousands of travelers and training nearly 5,000 health workers in case it crossed the borders. Then Ebola arrived. A man who had been ill for weeks and was later confirmed to have Ebola left eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), crossed by road into neighboring Uganda and flew to Nairobi, passing airport health screening in both countries without being flagged. A relative and a friend drove him directly from the airport to the Nairobi Hospital, a private hospital in the Kenyan capital. By the time he arrived on October 3, he had a fever, chills, severe fatigue, muscle pain and bleeding beneath his skin, according to Kenya’s Ministry of Health. Doctors isolated him and tests later confirmed Bundibugyo virus, a form of Ebola. He died days later on Monday, and health officials have been trying to identify anyone who may have been exposed. His journey shows how quickly an outbreak centered in the DRC can become a wider regional problem. The outbreak is now the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country. As of Wednesday, the World Health Organization (WHO) had recorded 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 deaths in the DRC. Cases have been recorded across seven provinces. WHO says transmission remains intense and assesses the risk to countries sharing land borders with the DRC as high. The DRC is not the only country affected. Uganda recorded 20 cases before its health ministry declared the country Ebola-free on July 28, while France recorded a travel-related case with no additional cases reported. Kenya is now the fourth country to confirm Bundibugyo virus. Oyewale Tomori, a former WHO regional virologist for Africa, told CNN that the Kenya case warns that more infections could cross borders while transmission remains high in the DRC. “Africa is an open field divided into countries by poorly manned porous borders,” he said. “The Kenya case is a warning of more cases in the future.” Why cross-border spread is hard to stop The Kenyan man, who had lived in the DRC for seven years, moved through three countries in about two days. On October 2, he traveled by road through Beni in eastern DRC’s North Kivu province to Kampala, Uganda’s capital, before flying to Nairobi the next day, according to Kenya’s Ministry of Health and WHO. Authorities have not said what screening, if any, he underwent at the DRC-Uganda land border. WHO says it is unclear when he developed Ebola symptoms during the trip. The agency says his month-long illness suggests he was probably sick with something else at first and possibly later contracted Ebola while seeking care. Uganda had temporarily restricted non-essential travel across its border with the DRC after most of its cases were imported from the country. Uganda’s health ministry said the man spent fewer than 24 hours in the country and had a normal temperature when screened before departing Entebbe International Airport, near Kampala. The ministry said it was intensifying cross-border surveillance and information sharing following the case. In Nairobi, Kenya’s health ministry says he underwent “normal public health screening” at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. The ministry’s account indicates he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola case during the screening. Kenya Airports Authority told CNN that Port Health Services, part of the Ministry of Health, handles passenger screening. CNN has asked health authorities in Uganda and Kenya what checks he underwent and whether his recent travel from the DRC should have prompted further assessment. The challenge goes beyond airports and official border crossings. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) told CNN that movement between Ebola-affected parts of eastern DRC and neighboring countries remains high, with people regularly crossing for work, trade and family reasons. Not all of that movement happens through official border posts. IOM said some people use informal routes that are much harder to monitor, so airport and land-border screening will not catch every infected traveler, especially before symptoms appear. It said countries also need to watch for cases in communities, test quickly, trace contacts and share information across borders – just like the response in Kenya – so imported cases are found early and further spread can be contained. Why health screening can miss cases Tomori was skeptical that border screening alone could do much, comparing weaknesses in the system to “using a football goalpost net to catch a mosquito.” Christian Happi, a professor of molecular biology and genomics at Redeemer’s University in Nigeria, whose laboratory helped confirm Nigeria’s first Ebola case in 2014, said temperature checks can miss an infected traveler who is not running a fever at that moment. “If you don’t have a fever at the time you are passing the health post at the airport, how is the health care worker going to detect it?” he asked. WHO’s current guidance for the DRC calls for exit screening at airports, ports and ground crossings, including at least a questionnaire about possible exposure and a temperature check. The agency says “suspected, probable and confirmed” cases, as well as contacts assessed as exposed, should not travel internationally except for medical evacuation. Happi argues that authorities should go further and require people flying from the DRC to show a negative Ebola test before boarding. “Anybody without a negative Ebola test should not board a flight,” he said. He also said countries need the capacity to test travelers much more quickly at airports. His proposal goes beyond WHO guidance, which does not call for negative Ebola tests for every traveler leaving an affected area. WHO also advises against broader travel or trade restrictions involving affected countries. CNN has asked WHO and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) how likely the outbreak is to spread further across borders and what countries should do as cases continue in the DRC. That is why the response doesn’t stop at the border: when screening misses a case, speed becomes critical. The bigger test: stopping onward spread In Kenya, health officials are now trying to identify anyone who may have been exposed and prevent further transmission. They have also intensified screening at Nairobi’s Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Preliminary tests on a separate 20-year-old patient who had traveled from the DRC through Uganda came back negative for Ebola on Thursday, according to Kenyan authorities. Rapid detection is particularly important because there is no licensed vaccine or approved specific treatment for this form of Ebola, although possible vaccines and treatments are being tested. Happi pointed to Nigeria’s experience during the 2014 West Africa Ebola epidemic, when an imported case in Lagos, one of Africa’s largest cities, led to 20 cases and eight deaths before transmission was stopped. He said rapid detection and close coordination were key to containing the outbreak. For Happi, Nigeria’s experience is the lesson for countries now watching the DRC outbreak. “It won’t be easy to detect everybody crossing borders,” he said. “It is how quickly countries detect and then how quickly they can contain imported cases.”

articles.title: India deploys police and restricts transport ahead of mass protest in Delhi
articles.summary: The Cockroach Janta Party wants Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to quit over changes to voter lists.
articles.body:
India has deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel in central Delhi and restricted transport in and around the capital ahead of a youth-led protest demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the country’s chief election commissioner.

Saturday’s rally, called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-based political movement, is expected to be the biggest yet in a wave of near-daily protests over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Organisers have billed it as a protest to “Save Democracy”.

Police have not authorised a rally at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which authorities usually designate for protests, because they said the request was not made on time and that the CJP had violated undertakings given during earlier protests .

Police have also warned that protesters will face a forceful law enforcement response if they violate the ban.

Roads to the site are blocked with multiple layers of metal barricades, as authorities shut 57 metro stations from Friday night, cancelled several long-distance trains and suspended mobile internet within 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area until Saturday night, the Indian news agency ANI reported.

India’s Supreme Court said on Friday that some trains must still run and that blanket closure of metro stations is unlikely.

“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” CJP chief Abhijeet Dipke said on X.

The CJP says at least 10,000 people, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.

“You can detain the people, you cannot detain the movement,” said Neha Bora, national president of the All India Students’ Association, who has emerged as a leading face of the protests.

Protesters want Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to quit over a voter list revision that has removed more than 130 million names.

The Election Commission says the exercise removes duplicate and ineligible voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from voting.

Critics say it has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities .

The protests escalated after the Indian Express reported that Kumar’s two deputies had formally raised concerns at least 14 times in the past 10 months over the revisions.

The Election Commission and the BJP have denied the allegations. The BJP says the opposition is misleading the country because it cannot win elections.

The CJP began online as political satire in May after Chief Justice Surya Kant called unemployed youth “cockroaches”, sparking nationwide outrage. Since then, the CJP has garnered a large following among India’s youth.

The July protests led Modi’s education minister to resign over exam paper leaks. The latest demonstrations come months before a series of state elections in early 2027, including in Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, which the BJP governs.

articles.title: Flydubai attacker began drifting towards extremism in Australia, UAE says
articles.summary: The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general also alleges the co-pilot was trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport.
articles.body:
The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai plane started a "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Australia, United Arab Emirates officials say.

UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi also alleged the pilot - widely named as Hamam al-Hammami - was last week trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport in a "suicide attack".

He wounded the captain in the cockpit with the emergency crash axe before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was able to land the aircraft in Saudi Arabia.

Melbourne university RMIT earlier confirmed the pilot had studied there but left before completing his engineering qualification.

According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001.

"The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday.

"During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks."

The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach".

"He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said.

The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving.

This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment".

More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September.

In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia.

The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia".

Indian co-pilot Capt Smit Machchhar has been hailed a hero after managing to unlock the cockpit door while being violently attacked with an axe, allowing passengers to get in and take control of the aircraft.

Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by Flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.

Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.

He was later hired by UAE-based Flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.

Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.

articles.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
articles.summary: After four years, a Ukrainian man is set to stand trial in Hamburg accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream pipelines.
articles.body:
Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.

Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.

But German police were already closing in on him.

After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.

Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".

Both he and his country have denied any involvement.

Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.

It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.

There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.

Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.

They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.

Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.

As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.

Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.

But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.

They went on following the forensic crumbs.

The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.

In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.

That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.

He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.

But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.

Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.

By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.

Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.

None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.

But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them.

"Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."

Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.

That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.

Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution.

"Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.

The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.

Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence.

"At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.

Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".

Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.

Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.

He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.

Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.

Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.

He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.

Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.

In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".

As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."

The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.

After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.

It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.

It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.

When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".

This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further.

"I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.

He argued that the Nord Stream pipelines had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed that to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe.

"Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."

Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.

Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.

Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.

He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.

His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.

And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.

His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.

I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.

articles.title: Queen reflects on reading 'forbidden' Lady Chatterley's Lover under the pillow
articles.summary: In BBC documentary The Book That Changed My Life, the Queen speaks about memorable moments in her own reading.
articles.body:
Queen Camilla has recalled secretly reading Lady Chatterley's Lover, the passionate and controversial novel by DH Lawrence, as a teenager in the 1960s.

"As teenagers you read a lot of romances. It was the moment of Lady Chatterley, under our pillows, reading that by torchlight. You know the minute something is forbidden, you want to get hold of it," she said about the novel that had been at the centre of an obscenity trial.

The Queen spoke about memorable moments in her own reading for BBC documentary The Book That Changed My Life, and about the life-changing power of literacy and books.

She gave a glimpse of how regular reading is part of her royal marriage: "It's like the best tonic in the world. My husband and I actually read before dinner, just sitting quietly and reading.

"He loves biographies, and PJ Wodehouse. I occasionally, when I'm deep in a book, hear him roaring with laughter about something," said the Queen about the King's affection for the author of the Jeeves and Wooster comic novels.

"It's very off-putting, I can't get back into my book, or I'll suddenly start weeping. But it's a lovely, quiet time. I think it would be a complete and utter tragedy if books went forever," she said.

The Queen also revealed more of her own youthful reading, saying she was "mesmerised" by Charles Dickens's Tale of Two Cities and its depiction of those watching the guillotine during the French Revolution.

"Those ghastly women sitting there knitting while everybody had their heads chopped off," she said.

The Queen, who is 79 years old, said she was part of a generation of women who missed out on higher education, which made reading and books even more important.

"I left school quite young. In my day, women didn't go to university, so I think reading has been most of my education," she said.

The documentary shows the impact of reading on people in stressful circumstances - and that includes Omar, who discovered a love of reading while in prison.

Reading was a way of escaping the confines of a cell, at least in his imagination - and the book he remembers most was a tattered copy of Jack Higgins's war thriller, The Eagle Has Landed.

Chatting to Omar after the screening of the documentary, he said that what struck him most about meeting the Queen was her "authenticity".

He said that off camera she was genuinely interested in his role working in prison education - helping a prison population that's facing chronic levels of illiteracy.

The pair also shared unexpected connections.

Camilla's father, Bruce Shand, had also been a prisoner, in a different kind of captivity, as a prisoner of war captured in North Africa during the Second World War.

He had used books as an emotional escape tunnel, during two and a half years of imprisonment.

"He said he educated himself. He read every single book, from the Bible to the encyclopedia, whatever was there, he just sat there all day long and read and read. And I think that's how he survived it," said the Queen.

She remembered how her father didn't want to talk about the war - "you bury it all because you've seen such horrendous things" - and so it was only when she read his memoir that she understood his experiences.

"It was written from the heart. I mean, I cried through most of it. I found it so moving. Because if you think, I didn't know anything about it, and reading managed to get him through it."

Omar said the Queen had recognised a connection.

"She talked about the parallels, her father found reading in a prisoner of war camp. She definitely recognised the resemblance… being in a place you don't want to be and using books to escape it and then books elevating you on many levels," he said.

Queen Camilla has been running her Queen's Reading Room project for five years, a kind of mega book club, with festivals and events and outreach projects, such as bringing books to homeless shelters.

It's part of her campaign to promote and protect the value of reading and to stop us becoming a culture of screen addicts.

Perhaps the most moving parts of the documentary are the stories of how books can become lifelines for people facing bereavement or intense loneliness.

Ian, from the north-east of England, spoke with heartbreaking candour about finding himself in a state of complete social isolation after the death of his mother.

"I used to sit with my head on the kitchen table, crying. It was such a difficult period of loneliness, of nothingness," he said.

Reading and becoming part of a book group proved a lifesaver for him, coaxing him back to his own happy ending.

There's a powerful testimony from Peter, a Merseyside truck driver, who had to admit that he wasn't able to read and needed help, after the shame of having to keep inventing excuses to his children who wanted a bedtime story.

He was taught to read by an adult education project - and he proudly shows the copy of JK Rowling's Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone that has become his own stepping stone to literacy.

Perhaps the most sobering statistic in this documentary is that there are eight million adults in the UK who struggle with even basic levels of literacy.

Speaking after the screening, Big Issue founder John Bird blamed the scourge of adult illiteracy on a long-term political failure in tackling the "inheritance of poverty".

"We did not educate the people who found education difficult - and I was one of them," he said, having learned to read as a youngster in prison.

"People were written off, now we're paying for that," he added.

On the Queen's literacy campaign, he said she provided an important symbolic focus. He likened it to how sales of the Big Issue increase when Prince William helps to sell the magazine for the homeless.

"You don't have to be a monarchist to buy into this idea - I wouldn't say that I was a monarchist, but I do believe in the power of certain personalities to enable a lot of people to say I'm going to get stuck into this," said Lord Bird.

"I think it's wonderful books change people's lives," said the Queen, having revealed some clues about how books have turned the pages of her own story.

The Book That Changed My Life, BBC2, 14 October, 21.00 and iPlayer.
