articles.title: What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?
articles.summary: People who have been adopted or are in care sometimes struggle to access family medical history which could be crucial to their own health.
articles.body:
When Aaliyah found a lump in her breast, she was anxious to find out if she had inherited an increased risk of cancer.

But because she had been removed from her biological parents at the age of seven months and later adopted, she had no way of accessing her family medical history.

"Not knowing anything about yourself genetically is terrifying," says the 26-year-old, "you can't even begin to imagine it."

The lump turned out to be non-cancerous, but it was one of many occasions when she found herself unable to answer questions about her biological family's health.

Aaliyah, now a trainee solicitor, spent years trying to source information from local authorities and eventually made an official data access request to Bradford Council, which removed her from her biological family as a baby.

She says the whole process took its toll.

"I would say bureaucratic hellscape is an understatement," she admits.

Days before Aaliyah's 25th birthday, a large unmarked envelope landed on the doormat of her home, in Birmingham.

"I rip it open, thinking it's an early birthday present," she says.

But what was inside was the response to her data request - pages and pages of her family history, including some medical details she had been painstakingly trying to track down for years.

The documents contained upsetting information alluding to the reason she was taken into care, alongside court records and a personal letter from her social worker.

"They were just given to me in a completely nondescript pile, and they contained completely earth-shattering information, of which I don't think I have ever recovered from," she says.

Aaliyah says knowing about her biological family's health could have helped her understand her own medical concerns.

"My biological mother struggled with eating disorders all her life," she says. "I had very severe anorexia in my teens and that would have been incredibly useful to know."

When a child is adopted in the UK, their NHS number - or equivalent health service identifier - is changed to protect their anonymity.

Their existing medical records should be merged with their new record, but this does not necessarily include their wider family medical history.

And while some local authorities offer specialist support for adoptees up to 21 or 25, the ease of access can vary across the country.

The BBC contacted Bradford Council, which said: "We are genuinely sorry that when Aaliyah received sensitive and personal information through her subject access request, we did not offer the support or signposting she needed. We recognise that we should have done more.

"Following Aaliyah's experience, we are strengthening our approach so that adults accessing their records are given clear information about the support available."

Bradford Children and Families Trust has now offered Aaliyah a meeting to further discuss her experience.

'I might never have known until it was too late'

For Dr Chris Tennyson, a delay in getting information about his birth father's health could have put his life at risk.

The 40-year-old clinical psychologist, from Belfast, was adopted as a baby in the 1980s to "a really loving mum and dad, [in a] really comfortable family home".

But in his 20s, he became increasingly curious about his biological origins. He met his birth mother, but his attempts to find out about his father stalled after social workers warned him off asking questions.

Eight years later, Chris tried to trace him again, but it wasn't until he was 33 that a meeting was finally arranged.

Then, on the afternoon the father and son were due to meet, a social worker approached Chris.

"There's something that I need to share with you," the social worker told him. "Your father wants me to let you know that there's a genetic medical condition within your family."

Government pledges 10,000 new foster care places in England

Rise in babies in care proceedings raises fears of unnecessary adoptions, experts tell BBC

A member of Chris's biological family died in 2000, when the condition came to light. At the time, other members of the family were offered testing. But Chris, who was then aged 14, was not contacted.

The condition, called malignant hyperthermia, causes a potentially life-threatening reaction to certain drugs used during anaesthesia.

While genes linked to it can run in families, not everyone who inherits one of these will necessarily experience a reaction with anaesthesia.

After undergoing genetic tests, Chris discovered his potential risk at the age of 37 - some 23 years after the condition had become known in his wider family.

He says a lack of understanding of how to support adopted adults resulted in the delay in him getting tested.

Chris, who now works with adoption and fostering services in Northern Ireland, says the lack of available information for adoptees is "a huge blind spot".

"There needs to be some kind of mechanism where adopted people's care records can be updated with family information that becomes available throughout the lifespan."

My daughter will have the knowledge I wish I had

First-time mum Courtney-Grace says she is relieved her baby daughter, Tine, will have access to the crucial family medical history she lacked when she grew up.

Now living in the North of England, the 28-year-old was adopted as a baby and spent time in foster care as a teenager.

"The only thing we knew about my medical history is my biological mom was mentally ill, and had depression."

In her mid-20s, Courtney-Grace was diagnosed with a genetic mutation, which can be inherited and is associated with an increased risk of tumours.

Her symptoms had previously been misdiagnosed as asthma and anxiety, which she says was based off the little doctors knew about her mum.

Courtney-Grace believes allowing medical professionals access to familial history without interfering with data protection rules wouldn't just benefit adoptees, but the entire population.

"The system needs a bit of an overhaul as a whole," she says.

'Adoption support not working well enough'

A government consultation on adoption support was launched in February 2026.

Josh MacAlister, the minister for children and families - who is responsible for adoption and children's social care in England - told the BBC that medical records was one of the issues being looked at.

"Adoption support and how it's set up at the moment isn't working well enough and there are obvious gaps in a number of areas that we're going to be looking at making changes to," MacAlister said.

He acknowledged that the current system did not strike the right balance between safeguarding biological relatives' medical privacy and enabling adopted people to access information relevant to their own health.

"We do need to change how we keep, retain, and share medical records," he said.

Authorities in England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales all make provisions for adoptees to access their medical history, but the way this operates in practice can vary hugely in the different nations.

None of the four nations gives patients the legal right to that information.

But they advise that when a new clinical record is created for an adopted child, enough information must be kept to support continuity of care.

NHS England said depending on the circumstances of an adoption there may be a need to "protect from disclosure any information about a third party".

But it added that it is important any new NHS records, if created, contain sufficient information to allow for a continuity of care.

For Courtney-Grace, her own diagnosis means her five-month-old daughter will now be closely monitored.

Cord blood was collected when Tine was born, and it will be tested for the genetic condition when she is five. If she has inherited it, a plan will be put in place.

"She has the medical information," Courtney-Grace says. "She can say, 'My mum has this'".

A list of organisations in the UK offering support and information with some of the issues in this story is available at BBC Action Line

articles.title: Taiwan president says defence spending boost aims to ‘deter war’
articles.summary: President Lai Ching-te emphasises peace and freedom, vows not to tolerate aggression in Taiwan Strait.
articles.body:
Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te has said the island “cherishes peace” and will “not give up our freedom” in a National Day speech outside the Presidential Office in Taipei.

Lai made the remarks on Saturday before thousands of people, including foreign diplomats.

“We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination,” he said. “Our aim by increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke; rather, it is to deter war.”

Taiwanese fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over the capital ahead of the speech.

The holiday marks the 115th anniversary of a 1911 uprising that toppled China’s last imperial dynasty and led to the founding of the Republic of China.

Taiwan’s 23 million people live under the constant threat of an attack by China, which insists the island is part of its territory, has never renounced the use of force to take it, and calls Lai a “separatist”.

Beijing has rebuffed his offers of talks.

Lai said China continued to “apply pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to alter the status quo across the Taiwan Strait”.

Grey-zone tactics are actions that stop short of open war. “Peace cannot rely solely on wishes, and tolerance cannot become a pretext for aggressors to encroach ever further,” he added.

Lai’s government has set aside a record 1.1 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($34.5bn) for defence in 2027, more than 3 percent of gross domestic product.

China held war games around the island shortly after Lai’s first National Day speech in 2024, but not last year. Its last drills near Taiwan were in late December, after news of an $11bn arms deal with Washington, the largest ever US weapons package for the island.

Lai said he welcomed talks between the United States and China, but insisted “there must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist”.

He urged democracies in the Indo-Pacific to join forces to preserve peace and stability in the region.

The US switched official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago but remains Taiwan’s most important security backer.

Officials in Washington and Taipei have repeatedly said US policy on Taiwan has not changed under President Donald Trump.

In May, after meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, Trump suggested arms sales to Taiwan could be a bargaining chip with China, which set off alarm across the world.

Taiwan is now waiting for Trump to sign off on $14bn worth of weapons, including the US-made Patriot air defence system.

The dispute dates back to China’s civil war, when the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after defeat by Mao Zedong’s communists.

The Republic of China remains the island’s formal name.

articles.title: Florida put radioactive fertiliser waste beneath a private road; 4 test sections are being monitored for safety
articles.summary: A waste material from fertiliser production is being tested for a new use in road construction in Florida.
articles.body: A waste material from fertiliser production is being tested for a new use in road construction in Florida. The material, known as phosphogypsum, is produced when phosphate ore is processed to make phosphoric acid. It contains radium, which can decay into radioactive radon gas, so its use is regulated by the US Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA generally requires phosphogypsum to be managed in engineered stacks that limit public exposure. However, some other uses can be approved when they provide at least as much protection.According to the US Environmental Protection Agency, one such project in New Wales, Florida, uses phosphogypsum in the road base beneath asphalt on private property. The agency determined that the project was as protective of human health as stacking the material.How will the Florida road project be monitored for safetyThe EPA approved a phosphogypsum road construction project for Mosaic Fertilizer, LLC on December 23, 2024. The project is located on private property in New Wales, Florida. Phosphogypsum will be incorporated into the road base and covered with asphalt. The test road has four sections containing phosphogypsum in the road base, separated by four control sections without phosphogypsum.One upgradient monitoring well and two downgradient wells will be placed in each section. The property has controlled access, so members of the public are not expected to come into contact with the phosphogypsum in the test road. The EPA approved the request after determining that the proposed use was as protective of human health as placement of phosphogypsum in a stack.Why is the material considered a radiation and health concernPhosphogypsum is produced when phosphate ore is processed to make phosphoric acid, which is later used in fertilizer. The phosphate ore and the resulting phosphogypsum contain radium. Radium decays to form radon gas, which is radioactive and can cause cancer.The EPA says radon in outside air can enter structures and reach levels that pose a health hazard over time. Higher exposure to radon over prolonged periods can increase the risk of developing lung cancer. Phosphogypsum stacks also contain low-pH process water and heavy metals. Because radionuclides in phosphogypsum are a source of radon gas and direct gamma radiation, the EPA regulates phosphogypsum as a source category of radionuclides under the Clean Air Act.How are stacks designed to limit exposureEPA regulations generally require phosphogypsum to be managed in engineered stacks to limit public exposure from radon emissions. Owners and operators of inactive stacks must measure and report radon emissions and keep those emissions within regulatory limits. When phosphogypsum is placed on a stack, it is added as a liquid slurry.As the stack dewaters, the liquid effluent is captured, treated, tested, and discharged under the Clean Water Act. Newer stacks contain a liner to help prevent effluent from being released directly into soil and groundwater, while older stacks may not. When inactive, an engineered cover is typically placed over the phosphogypsum to prevent further water infiltration.Other uses of phosphogypsum under EPA rulesEPA regulations allow phosphogypsum to be removed from stacks for outdoor agricultural purposes and indoor research and development under certain conditions and restrictions. Any other use requires prior EPA approval formally. The agency evaluates each proposed use case by case, considering how the phosphogypsum would be used, the amount involved, and possible health risks to workers and the public, including risks from handling and transportation. EPA can approve a proposed use only when it is at least as protective of public health as placing phosphogypsum in a stack.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Coco Rocha's 'full circle moment' as Ireland Fashion Week impresses
articles.summary: Now in its second year, Ireland Fashion Week takes place this week.
articles.body:
Canadian supermodel Coco Rocha has described Ireland's fashion scene as "amazing" and said a national fashion week "should have probably happened years ago", after making her first visit to the country.

Leading fashion industry figures, including activist and model Alana Hadid, descended on Slane Castle in County Meath earlier this week as Ireland Fashion Week got under way.

Now in its second year, more than 80 designers are taking part in the six-day event, which is billed as a showcase for Irish fashion, culture and creativity with shows, talks and exhibitions planned across the country.

Rocha, whose career spans more than 20 years, said modelling at the event felt like a "full circle moment", as she was first discovered at an Irish dancing competition as a teenager.

Despite growing up closely connected to her Irish heritage (on both sides of her family), and spending 18 years as a dancer, Rocha said she had never previously had the chance to visit the island.

"I'm very proud of, the fact that I am Irish, I am an Irish dancer, and it is the special thing about me, and so now it's exciting to bring myself here."

Rocha said she had been "truly wowed" by the scale and quality of homegrown design talent on display, and hopes the event will ensure creatives build successful careers without feeling they have to move abroad.

"I really hope that this does much more than just shine a light," she told BBC News NI. "That it actually really helps them to maybe stay here or to really figure out what's the next steps for them."

Rocha added: "They're not just sort of good. They're amazing."

While much of the fashion industry is focused on 'The Big Four' - London, Paris, Milan and New York - Rocha said smaller fashion weeks can benefit communities.

With a changing, digital-first industry, designers can be "really just honing their craft" at home, she added.

Comparing the event to TV show Project Runway, which Rocha hosts, she said it's important to "expose the next generation" to fashion and help them see "that this is local" and accessible.

"I think if we've done that, we've done a good job."

Now in its second year, the festival has expanded significantly since its 2025 launch and is a platform to help designers build opportunities at home and abroad.

An all-island event, several designers and brands from Northern Ireland are included in the programme.

It comes as Irish fashion is experiencing a breakthrough moment, with internationally-recognised designers like Sinéad O'Dwyer, Simone Rocha and Jonathan Anderson referencing their heritage in their collections.

In December, prestigious French fashion house Dior- steered by Magherafelt-born Anderson - will be holding its first runway show in Ireland.

Ireland Fashion Week founder Ashley McDonnell said this year's event is focused on "building on the momentum" of 2025 and demonstrating what can be achieved when Irish fashion is viewed as an industry rather than a series of individual successes.

She said the island has "extraordinary designers", but that talent must be matched by "building an ecosystem" of investment, commercial opportunities, international exposure and stronger support structures.

This year's programme reflects that ambition. Alongside runway shows, it includes industry discussions, graduate showcases and networking events designed to connect designers with buyers, investors and international media.

Among those taking part was County Tyrone designer Sarah Jayne Lavery, founder of Charlotte & Tess, based in the Linen Green in Moy, and its in-house label Atelier, which launched just two years ago.

Speaking after showing her collection as part of the event's Irish Roots presentation, she described the experience as a milestone.

"Having my own brand and designing is genuinely a dream of mine," she told BBC News NI.

Lavery was one of 11 designers selected for the showcase following an application and interview process.

Her collection featured Irish materials including Donegal tweed, Aran wool and linen, reflecting the show's focus on heritage and craftsmanship.

Discovering Hadid would be wearing one of her designs was an unexpected highlight.

"She was our final look. I didn't know that she was walking for me until I arrived... I was just delighted," she explained.

The designer believes events like Ireland Fashion Week help to change perceptions of the industry and put creatives on "an international stage".

"I think Ireland is a really creative space at the moment. I think it's very exciting," she said.

She said organisers were shining a spotlight on Irish talent and putting "fashion at the forefront".

The theme of this year's event was 'Coming Home', celebrating Irish creativity, heritage and the designers returning to showcase their work.

"We have so much talent and creativity here, we have so many beautiful fabrics that lots of the designers are using.

"I would encourage any Irish designer to get involved next year."

The next generation of fashion talent is also taking centre stage at the event, with Belfast-based knitwear designer Grace Bowman "honoured" to be among 44 creatives selected for the graduate runway showcase.

"That extra support, that extra exposure, the networking – it's all so important to build a community here in Ireland, as well as spreading our design around. We're really making everyone have access to Irish design," she said.

The 22-year-old, who launched her own label after studying at Ulster University and completing a placement with Inis Meáin Knitting Company, draws inspiration from the Irish landscape and traditional Irish craftsmanship.

Bowman will present her collection which combines deadstock linen and organic cotton with abstract Celtic knot motifs and hand-embroidered details.

She said it's "so important" to look back on traditional techniques and "embrace them" alongside contemporary design methods.

"I'm from Belfast so the linen industry has such an historical impact here. It's great to be able to use that within my work and really have Irish materials supported within our industry," she said.

"I'm very excited to see everyone else's work on the runway... It will be a fantastic showcase of Irish design and an amazing platform for emerging designers."

articles.title: US hosts ‘productive’ trilateral talks to end Russia-Ukraine war
articles.summary: US envoy Steve Witkoff says renewed negotiations aim to ensure lasting peace before winter approaches.
articles.body:
United States, Ukrainian and European officials have met in Miami, Florida, to discuss a proposal for ⁠ending the Russia-Ukraine war, US envoy Steve Witkoff said in a statement posted to X.

Witkoff said on Friday that “constructive discussions” tackled “potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace”.

Witkoff said the meeting included “the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO”.

The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and “longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflict”, Witkoff said.

He also noted the “productive” talks discussed “Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday the conflict had reached a dangerous “stalemate” , with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.

“The other way that stalemates end is through escalation,” Rubio told reporters, warning that the conflict could spread to neighbouring NATO countries.

Earlier on Friday, Russian President Vladimir Putin told US President Donald Trump that the resumption of talks with Ukraine is unlikely , citing drone attacks on Moscow during parliamentary elections last month.

The renewed diplomacy comes against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks, including a strike on civilian buses in eastern Ukraine that killed 33 people. Authorities said the attack was the single deadliest attack this year.

The ongoing talks have been overshadowed by the US-Russia diesel deal on Friday. Trump blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries for surging diesel prices.

The deal was criticised by US lawmakers, Zelenskyy and European allies.

Zelenskyy called the agreement a “gift to Putin”. Hours after the deal, a Ukrainian drone hit a Russian fuel site.

The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.

articles.title: Weetabix plans major revamp of its Northamptonshire HQ built in 1932
articles.summary: Plans include redeveloping its Brooklands warehouse site in Burton Latimer to make way for a new office building.
articles.body:
Breakfast cereal giant Weetabix has submitted a planning application to upgrade its headquarters, which date back to 1932.

The proposals include the redevelopment of its former Brooklands warehouse site and ancillary buildings in Burton Latimer, North Northamptonshire, to make way for a new office building.

North Northamptonshire Council received the application on 29 September. The proposals also include changes to car parking, servicing, landscaping and ancillary works.

Weetabix has also invited people to have their say on the plans.

The planning statement said the proposals, "will utilise previously developed land of the former 'Brooklands warehouse', its ancillary buildings and associated hardscape.

"The built structures will be demolished to allow for the development of the hub."

The offices in the current headquarters will no longer be used once the new hub is operational.

articles.title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
articles.summary: The Pentagon says the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, but experts suggest officials are reading the country wrong.
articles.body:
They came in their thousands from near and far - men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.

It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heat wave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators.

By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.

That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.

The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.

Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.

That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.

By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.

A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan , who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.

The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad would be live-streamed.

"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.

University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked.

"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told BBC.

He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining; it was 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%.

"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.

It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's nearly certain that millions or more will tune in.

With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment … bring your popcorn, invite your friends".

Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream.

"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up … to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."

Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's 2002 death, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.

The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution.

"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."

But the polarisation and rhetoric in American politics may have, in some way, perhaps set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University.

"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't, and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution; they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"

Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.

Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said survey data points to a declining appetite for violence in the US.

"This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labeled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people."

"I think it's this: A public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."

Vice-President JD Vance, a Catholic, has said he would not be watching the execution .

President Donald Trump dodged the question of whether he'd tune in himself - but confirmed he approved the decision to livestream Hasan's death.

"I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."
